title: LLaMA: Open & Efficient Foundation Models
hook: You don't need a 175B-parameter model to compete. LLaMA trained smaller models on lots of public data — and lit a fire under the open-weights community.
key_points: A family of comparatively small LLMs (7B to 65B parameters).
Trained only on publicly available data, no proprietary corpora.
Smaller LLaMA models rivaled or beat much larger ones on many benchmarks.
Following Chinchilla, it trained longer on more tokens for efficiency.
Its release energized open-weights, on-device, and fine-tuned model work.
content_html: LLaMA, from Touvron, Lavril, and colleagues at Meta in 2023, is a family of foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters, trained entirely on publicly available data. The key result: these comparatively small models matched or beat much larger ones on many benchmarks, proving that careful training beats raw size. Their release became a catalyst for the open-weights ecosystem.
extra_html:
How it works

Taking the Chinchilla lesson to heart, the team trained relatively small models on a large number of tokens — spending more compute during training so the finished model is cheaper to run. They used only public datasets and a standard decoder-only Transformer with some efficiency tweaks. The payoff is a model that fits on accessible hardware while staying competitive in quality.

Why it matters

Big, capable models had largely been locked behind APIs. LLaMA showed strong models could be small enough to run, study, and fine-tune more widely, and its weights spread fast through the research community. That sparked a wave of open fine-tuned variants, on-device experiments, and tooling. It helped shift the conversation from "scale at any cost" toward accessible, efficient models.

related.title: Chinchilla: Compute-Optimal Scaling
related.hook: Most giant models were starved of data. Chinchilla showed that for a fixed compute budget you should grow parameters and tokens together — and a smaller, longer-trained model won.
